article.headline: Three.js Showcases Real-Time Skeletal Animation in Browser
article.lede: A screenshot from Reze Studio, a web-based 3D animation tool built on Three.js, demonstrates the library's ability to handle complex skeletal rigging and motion-capture playback entirely in the browser. The image shows a character model with 147 bones, morph targets, and an imported VMD animation file (miku.vmd) running at 60 FPS.
article.body:
Three.js, the open-source JavaScript 3D library maintained by Mr.doob (Ricardo Cabello), has long been the go-to tool for browser-based 3D graphics. This screenshot from Reze Studio—a third-party editor built on Three.js—illustrates how far the ecosystem has come. The interface displays a character rig with 147 bones, subdivided into upper body, arms, hands, and lower body, alongside morph targets for facial expressions. An imported VMD animation file (miku.vmd), a format popularized by the Vocaloid software for Miku Hatsune, is being played back at 60 frames per second.

The key technical achievement here is the real-time interpolation of skeletal animation. The property panel shows rotation, translation, and interpolation curves (linear, in/out) for each bone, with a timeline scrubber at the bottom. This level of control—typically found in desktop applications like Blender or Maya—is now possible in a web browser thanks to Three.js's efficient rendering pipeline and the underlying WebGL API. The fact that a 147-bone rig with morph targets can animate smoothly at 60 FPS in a browser window speaks to the maturity of both the library and modern GPU-accelerated web standards.

Reze Studio itself is a notable example of the growing trend toward browser-based creative tools. By leveraging Three.js, it avoids the need for installation or powerful local hardware, making 3D animation accessible to anyone with a modern browser. The tool's integration with VMD format also highlights the cross-pollination between the Vocaloid fan community and professional-grade 3D workflows. While Three.js is not the only WebGL library—rivals like Babylon.js (owned by Microsoft (MSFT)) offer similar capabilities—its simplicity and massive community have made it the de facto standard for web-based 3D experimentation.

concepts.definition: A technique in computer animation where a character is represented by a hierarchical set of bones (the skeleton) and a surface mesh. Each bone influences a portion of the mesh, and animating the bones moves the mesh accordingly, enabling realistic movement with fewer keyframes.

Also known as blend shapes, a technique where a base mesh is deformed into predefined shapes (e.g., facial expressions) by interpolating vertex positions. Used alongside skeletal animation for fine-grained control.

A file format used by the Vocaloid software to store motion data for 3D characters, particularly associated with the virtual singer Hatsune Miku. It contains bone keyframes and camera movements, and is widely used in the MikuMikuDance community.

A JavaScript API for rendering interactive 2D and 3D graphics within any compatible web browser without the use of plug-ins. It is based on OpenGL ES and is the foundation for libraries like Three.js.

repos.summary: The official repository for Three.js, a cross-browser JavaScript library and API used to create and display animated 3D computer graphics in a web browser. It is the most popular WebGL library, with over 100k stars on GitHub.
